904.title: leaving Vrindavan
904.carry: in the river, and in the chariot
904.howItsDone: Akrura's hymn in the Bhagavata is recited by devotees, and pilgrims bathe at a place on the Yamuna that tradition links with his vision.

segments.voice: Yesterday: leaving Vrindavan, from the side of the ones who stay. The gopis in the road, a promise to come back, and the dust settling.

On the road to Mathura, the chariot stops at the river. Akrura asks the boys to wait in the shade while he goes down to the Yamuna to bathe and say his prayers. He wades in, ducks under, and opens his eyes. Krishna and Balarama are there, under the river, looking at him. Which is strange, because he just left them sitting in the chariot.
screen: `THE CHARIOT STOPS AT THE RIVER.` → `AKRURA DUCKS UNDER.` → `THE BOYS ARE IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Akrura does what anyone would do. He comes up for air and looks back at the bank. There's the chariot, and the two boys sitting in it, just as he left them. So he goes under again, and this time the vision is bigger. He sees Balarama as the great serpent Ananta, and resting on him, Vishnu himself, dark as a rain cloud, dressed in yellow, with sages and gods around him singing his praise. Akrura stays there in the river, and the Bhagavata gives him a long hymn of praise. Then he climbs out, dripping, and walks back to the chariot in a daze. Krishna asks him, kindly, whether he's seen something wonderful, in the earth or the sky or the water. Akrura answers that every wonder in the earth, the sky and the water is in Krishna, and he's looking at him. Why put this scene here? The whole village has just watched Krishna leave; the gopis stood in the road until the dust was gone. And soon after, a man discovers that the one he's driving to Mathura is also in the river, and also beyond all of it. The leaving is real; nobody in the story pretends it isn't. But the Bhagavata sets this vision right beside the grief, and some readers hear in it that the one who left the village hasn't left anything. They reach Mathura as the day ends. Krishna sends Akrura on ahead, and walks into the city on foot, with the cowherds.
screen: `ON THE CHARIOT, AND IN THE RIVER.` · `VISHNU RESTING ON ANANTA.` · `EVERY WONDER IS IN YOU.` · then, large: `HE HASN'T LEFT ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, the way Akrura did before he went under, and let the breath be slow, like water. Picture something ordinary you'll see again today, a kitchen, a street, a face, and look at it as if you'd just come up from the river and found it still there. If you pray, ask to see God, or Krishna, in what's right in front of you.
Leaving Vrindavan. The journey to Mathura, where Akrura sees the boys on the chariot, and also in the river, and Vishnu beyond them.
Your line: in the river, and in the chariot. Akrura looked twice and saw more. That's day nine hundred four.

905.title: Kamsa's death
905.howItsDone: The story of Krishna in Mathura and Kamsa's end is recited from the Bhagavata and staged in Krishna plays and festivals in the region of Mathura and Vrindavan.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last of leaving Vrindavan. Akrura went under the river and found the boys there, and in the chariot at once.
screen: `LEAVING VRINDAVAN.` · `IN THE RIVER, AND IN THE CHARIOT.`

segments.voice: King Kamsa can't sleep. That afternoon, word reached the palace that a cowherd boy walked into the festival hall, snapped the great bow on display, and fought off the guards. Now it's night, and everything Kamsa looks at seems wrong. The Bhagavata lists his omens. He looks at his reflection and can't see his head. He can't hear his own breath. He looks back for his footprints and finds none. The man who has spent the whole story hunting a child is now hunted, by his own mind.
screen: `THE GREAT BOW SNAPPED.` → `KAMSA CAN'T SLEEP.` → `NO HEAD IN THE REFLECTION.`

segments.voice: Morning brings the festival. Kamsa takes his seat on a high platform above the wrestling ground, ringed by his ministers and vassal kings. The citizens fill the stands. His champion wrestlers are ready. And at the gate he's stationed a huge war elephant with orders to crush the boys. It doesn't work. Krishna fights the elephant, brings it down, and walks into the arena with one of its tusks on his shoulder, Balarama beside him. Then the Bhagavata stops the action and looks around the stands, one face at a time. To the wrestlers, Krishna looks like a thunderbolt. To the men of the city, the finest of men. To the women, love itself in a body. To the cowherds who came with him, their own kinsman. To unjust rulers, the one who will punish them. To his parents, their child. To the yogis, the highest truth. To his own clan, their deity. And to Kamsa, the text says, he looks like death. Same boy, same moment, same dusty arena. What each person sees depends on what each one brought in. The wrestlers came for a fight, and they see a weapon. Kamsa brought a lifetime of fear, and fear is what walks in. Some readers take the scene as a teaching in a single picture: Krishna is met according to the heart that meets him.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT AT THE GATE.` · `A TUSK ON HIS SHOULDER.` · `ONE BOY, MANY EYES.` · then, large: `TO KAMSA, HE LOOKS LIKE DEATH.`

906.title: Kamsa's death
906.howItsDone: Kamsa's death and the freeing of Devaki and Vasudeva are retold from the Bhagavata, and Kamsa's defeat is acted out in festival performances in the Mathura area.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kamsa's death began. A sleepless king, an elephant at the gate, and one boy in the arena seen many ways, and by Kamsa, as death.

The women in the stands aren't happy. Down on the wrestling ground, Kamsa's champion Chanura has squared off against Krishna, and his partner Mushtika against Balarama: grown men built like mountains, against two boys from the cow pastures. The Bhagavata lets us hear the crowd. This is wrong, the women tell each other. It's no fair match. Whoever allowed it shares the blame. And the cowherd girls of Vraja were lucky, they say, to see him every day.
screen: `CHANURA AND MUSHTIKA.` → `TWO BOYS AGAINST GIANTS.` → `THE CROWD SAYS, THIS IS WRONG.`

segments.voice: The fight goes hold for hold, then turns. Krishna brings down Chanura, Balarama brings down Mushtika, and the other wrestlers fall or run. The arena erupts. Kamsa orders the music stopped. He shouts for the boys to be driven out of the city, the cowherds' goods seized and Nanda arrested, and Krishna's father Vasudeva and his own father Ugrasena killed. Before he finishes, Krishna is on the platform. Kamsa reaches for his sword. Krishna catches him by the hair, pulls him down into the arena, and it's over. Then the Bhagavata says something hard to forget. All his life, eating, drinking, walking, sleeping, Kamsa thought of Krishna, out of fear. And because his mind was so fixed on him, the text says, he reached him in the end. It's the frame from the rasa lila: what matters is where the mind is turned, even by terror. The story doesn't end only in triumph. Kamsa's wives come weeping, and Krishna comforts them and sees the funeral rites done. Then he goes to free his parents, Vasudeva and Devaki, whom Kamsa had chained again. He frees them and bows at their feet. So this part closes where it began. The birth in a prison cell. The crossing of the Yamuna in the storm. Putana, the butter thief, the mouth full of the universe. Kaliya, Govardhan, the flute, the moonlit dance, the road out of Vrindavan. And now the cell door open, and a son kneeling before his mother.
screen: `THE WRESTLERS FALL.` · `HE WAS NEVER NOT THINKING OF HIM.` · `KAMSA'S WIVES ARE COMFORTED.` · then, large: `THE PRISON DOOR OPENS.`

907.title: the Alvars (Andal, Nammalvar)
907.hook: a girl tries on the garland meant for the god
907.howItsDone: Andal is honored as one of the Alvars in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes; at Srivilliputtur, tradition holds that a garland worn by her image is still offered to the Lord.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kamsa's death. The king whose fear kept his mind on Krishna all his life, and a prison door opening for Devaki and Vasudeva.

A garland of fresh flowers lies ready in a temple gardener's house, woven that morning for the image of Vishnu. While her father is out, his daughter picks it up and puts it around her own neck. Then she leans over to see her reflection and asks herself: would he want me? The he, for her, is the god the garland was made for. Today the path leaves the Bhagavata's village and meets the people who sang about it, starting in the Tamil south.
screen: `A GARLAND FOR THE GOD.` → `SHE TRIES IT ON FIRST.` → `WOULD HE WANT ME?`

segments.voice: The Alvars are the poet-saints of Vishnu who sang in Tamil. Tradition counts twelve, and explains the name as people immersed, sunk deep in God, the way you sink into water over your head. Their songs aren't theology lectures. They're love songs, complaints, lullabies, longing. The girl with the garland is one of them: Andal. Her father, himself remembered as one of the Alvars, tends a flower garden for the temple. Tradition says he found her there as a baby, under a tulasi plant, and raised her as his own. She grows up on his stories of Krishna, and decides she will marry no one but the Lord. So she wears the garland before it goes to the temple. One day her father catches her. He's horrified: a garland someone has worn can't be offered to God. He throws it out and weaves a new one. That night, the story says, the Lord comes to him in a dream and asks why the usual garland didn't arrive. The one she wore is the one he wants. From then on her garlands go to the temple after she's worn them, and she gets a name for it: the girl who gave the garland she had worn. Sit with how strange that is. The rule of offering says fresh and untouched. The story says God prefers flowers already warm against the neck of someone who loved him enough to try them on. Nammalvar, the other name in today's title, comes the day after tomorrow.
screen: `THE ALVARS: POETS SUNK DEEP IN GOD.` · `A BABY UNDER THE TULASI PLANT.` · `HER FATHER THROWS THE GARLAND OUT.` · `THE ONE SHE WORE IS THE ONE HE WANTS.`

908.title: the Alvars (Andal, Nammalvar)
908.hook: girls knocking on doors in the dark, waking each other up
908.howItsDone: During the Tamil month of Margazhi, Andal's Tiruppavai is sung before dawn in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes, and the day's verse is often recited in morning worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alvars, and Andal, the gardener's daughter who wore the garland first. In the story, the Lord asked for the worn one.

It's still dark, cold enough that nobody wants to leave the blanket. A group of girls goes from house to house, rapping on doors and calling through windows to friends still asleep. Get up. The birds are already talking. You said you'd come. Are you deaf, or just pretending? One friend gets teased for bragging yesterday that she'd be first awake. This isn't a diary. It's a poem: Andal's song cycle, the Tiruppavai.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, IN THE COLD.` → `KNOCKING ON FRIENDS' DOORS.` → `ANDAL'S TIRUPPAVAI.`

segments.voice: The Tiruppavai is set in the Tamil month of Margazhi, in the cold season. Andal imagines herself as one of the cowherd girls of Krishna's village, the same village we just left in the Bhagavata. The girls have taken a vow for the month: rise before dawn, bathe, keep simple, and go together to seek him. So the songs move like a morning. First they gather. Then they wake the girls who overslept, door by door, affectionate and funny, the way friends really talk. They arrive at the house of Nanda, Krishna's foster father. They wake the doorkeeper, then Nanda, then Yashoda, then Krishna's brother. At last they stand before Krishna and tell him why they've come. On the surface, for a drum, a ritual drum for their vow. Then the songs turn. The drum was an excuse. What they want is to belong to him, to serve him, not just today but in every life to come. Notice who's seeking here. Not a lone hermit in a cave: a gang of friends dragging each other out of bed, refusing to go without the one still asleep. In Andal's picture, nobody gets to the door alone, and nobody's left behind for being lazy. They just knock louder. That's why these songs aren't only read. In Margazhi, people in Tamil homes and temples sing them before sunrise. A poem about getting up became a reason to get up.
screen: `THE COLD MONTH OF MARGAZHI.` · `WAKING THE GIRLS WHO OVERSLEPT.` · `AT NANDA'S DOOR.` · `NOT A DRUM, BUT TO BELONG TO HIM.`

909.title: the Alvars (Andal, Nammalvar)
909.hook: a silent boy under a tamarind tree, and a riddle that wakes him
909.carry: it will eat that, and lie there
909.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas recite Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli in temple worship and at home, and the tamarind tree at his temple town is honored as the place where he sat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alvars again. Andal's Tiruppavai, girls knocking on doors before dawn so nobody went to Krishna alone.

A man is walking south, following a light. That's how the story tells it: far away in the north on pilgrimage, he sees a glow in the southern sky that no one else seems to notice. He follows it a long way, to a temple town in the Tamil country, to a tamarind tree, and to a young man sitting in a hollow at its foot. Eyes closed. Not speaking. People there say he's been that way since he was a baby. The traveler has one question for him, and it's a riddle.
screen: `A LIGHT IN THE SOUTHERN SKY.` → `A TAMARIND TREE.` → `A YOUNG MAN WHO NEVER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: The young man is Nammalvar, the second name in our title. The traveler is Madhurakavi. Tradition says Nammalvar was born and didn't cry, didn't nurse, didn't open his eyes, and his worried parents left him at the temple, where he sat under the tamarind, growing up in stillness. Madhurakavi wants to know if anyone is home behind those closed eyes. So he asks, roughly: if a small thing is born inside something dead, what will it eat, and where will it lie? And for the first time, the story says, Nammalvar answers. It will eat that, and it will lie there. Two short lines, and Madhurakavi falls at his feet, his disciple for life. What did they mean? One traditional reading: the small thing is the living self, born into a body that by itself is lifeless matter. Until it turns to God, it feeds on that body's pleasures and pains, and stays there. Other teachers take the riddle further, or differently; the tradition lets it stay a little open. Then the silent one starts to sing. His songs, gathered as the Tiruvaymoli, are full of longing for Vishnu. In some, he speaks as a girl pining for her absent lover, and her mother and friends speak about her. Sri Vaishnava tradition holds these songs so high it calls them the Tamil Veda. And Madhurakavi is remembered among the Alvars too, for a short poem in praise of no one but his teacher.

910.title: the Nayanars
910.hook: a hunter who worships Shiva all wrong, and all right
910.howItsDone: Shaiva Hindus in Tamil Nadu honor the Nayanars in temples, often with images of them in a row, and Kannappa is especially remembered at the Shiva temple of Srikalahasti.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alvars once more. Nammalvar, silent under the tamarind, answered a riddle in two short lines, and then began to sing.
screen: `THE ALVARS.` · `IT WILL EAT THAT, AND LIE THERE.`

segments.voice: Every morning a priest climbs a hill to a small shrine of Shiva, and every morning he finds a mess. Bits of meat on the stone. Flowers that look like they've been stuck in somebody's hair. Water splashed everywhere, as if someone spat it. He cleans it all, does the worship properly, and goes home upset. Next morning, the same. Someone is worshiping here, and doing it all wrong.
screen: `A MESS AT SHIVA'S SHRINE.` → `EVERY MORNING, THE SAME.` → `WHO IS DOING THIS?`

segments.voice: Today the path crosses to the Nayanars, the Tamil saints of Shiva. Tradition counts sixty-three, and their lives are told in a long Tamil work, the Periya Puranam. They're a mixed crowd: kings and housewives, a potter, a washerman, a hunter. Today's is the hunter, Tinnan. Tracking in the hills, he comes across the shrine, and something in him breaks open. He has no idea how worship is done, so he does what a hunter would do for someone he loves. He carries water in his mouth, because he has no pot. He brings flowers in his hair, because his hands hold his bow. And he brings meat he has roasted and tasted first, so only the best goes to Shiva. That's the mess. In the story, Shiva tells the priest in a dream to hide and watch. So the priest is crouched behind the shrine the day the image's eye starts to bleed. Tinnan tries herbs. Nothing. So he takes an arrow, digs out his own eye, and presses it into place. The bleeding stops. Then the image's other eye starts to bleed. Tinnan sets his foot on the spot, so he can find it once he's blind, and lifts the arrow to his second eye. And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and stops him. From then on, the story says, he's called Kannappa, a name tied to his eye. There's a thread here. Krishna's village loved him without a rulebook. Andal wore the garland first. Now a hunter tastes the meat first. Again and again, love breaks the rule of the untouched offering, and the priest who knows every rule is the one sent to watch.
screen: `THE NAYANARS: SAINTS OF SHIVA.` · `WATER IN HIS MOUTH, MEAT TASTED FIRST.` · `HIS OWN EYE FOR THE BLEEDING ONE.` · `SHIVA'S HAND STOPS HIM.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open and think of the clumsiest way you've ever shown love: a burnt meal, a gift that missed, words that came out wrong. Look at it the way the story looks at Tinnan, seeing what you were actually trying to give, and let it be enough. If you pray, offer whatever you have today, clumsy as it is, to God by any name you use.
The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva, whose lives the Periya Puranam tells. Kannappa is the hunter who offered his own eye.
Your line: Kannappa's eye. A hunter with no rulebook, remembered as a saint. Day nine hundred ten, done.
